title: Fonts and Text
summary: Typography means the choices that shape how text looks, such as font, size and line spacing.
introduction: Typography means the choices that shape how text looks, such as font, size and line spacing. Make a paragraph easy to read. Try larger letters and more space between lines before adding decorative styles.
learningObjectives: Write a font-family stack with a generic fallback and load a web font with @font-face
Set font-size, font-weight, line-height and the font shorthand
Control alignment, decoration, transformation and spacing of text

blocks.text: `font-family` takes a list. The browser uses the first font in the list that is installed on the reader's device, which is why the list should end with a *generic family* (`serif`, `sans-serif`, `monospace`, `system-ui`) that always exists. Quote names that contain spaces. `system-ui` picks the operating system's own interface font, which looks native and costs no download.

blocks.text: An `@font-face` rule names a font and tells the browser where to download it. Use the `woff2` format (smallest, supported everywhere), self-host the file next to your CSS, and declare the weights it covers; a *variable* font covers a whole range in one file. `font-display: swap` shows the fallback font immediately and swaps in the web font when it arrives, instead of leaving the text invisible while it loads. Then use the family name in a normal `font-family` list with fallbacks behind it.

blocks.title: fonts.css

blocks.text: `font-size` is best written in `rem` so it scales with the user's settings (see [Units](/tutorials/css/units)). `font-weight` runs from 100 to 900; `400` is normal and `700` is bold, and the keywords `normal` and `bold` map to those two. If a font does not ship a weight you ask for, the browser picks the nearest one or synthesises a fake bold, which looks smudged, so check which weights your font provides. `font-style: italic` works the same way. The `font` shorthand sets style, weight, size, line height and family in one go; size and family are mandatory, and everything you omit is reset.

blocks.text: Two numbers do more for readability than any font choice. `line-height` is the distance between baselines; `1.5` to `1.6` suits body text and `1.1` to `1.25` suits large headings, where the default spacing looks loose. Write it as a unitless number, which means "this many times the element's own font size", so headings and paragraphs each get a proportional value from a single rule. Line *length* matters as much: 45 to 75 characters per line is comfortable, and `max-width: 65ch` enforces it in any font.

blocks.title: Do not set line-height in pixels on the body
blocks.text: `body { line-height: 24px; }` looks fine for paragraphs, but every heading inherits the same 24px: a 40px heading that wraps onto two lines overlaps itself. A unitless `line-height: 1.5` is inherited as a *factor* and recomputed from each element's own font size, so headings stay readable without extra rules.

`text-align` accepts `left`, `right`, `center` and `justify`; avoid `justify` on the web, where the lack of hyphenation leaves rivers of white space. `text-decoration` adds or removes underlines; keep the underline on links inside running text, where it is the main cue that something is clickable, and tune it with `text-decoration-thickness` and `text-underline-offset`. `text-transform: uppercase` is for short labels and pairs with a little `letter-spacing`. `white-space: nowrap` stops wrapping, and combined with `overflow: hidden` and `text-overflow: ellipsis` it truncates a single line with a trailing ellipsis.

blocks.code:
Field notes

Why line length matters more than the font

A line of sixty characters lets the eye travel back to the start of the next line without losing its place. Longer lines tire readers; shorter ones break the rhythm of the sentence.

questions.question: Why should a `font-family` list end with a generic family such as `sans-serif`?
questions.explanation: The browser walks the list and uses the first available font. A generic family is always available, so the text is guaranteed a sensible fallback.
options: It makes the first font load faster
It guarantees a usable font when none of the named fonts is installed
Generic families are required by the CSS validator
It enables bold and italic styles

questions.question: `font-weight: bold` and `font-weight: 700` request the same weight.
questions.explanation: The keyword `bold` maps to 700 and `normal` maps to 400 on the numeric scale.
